title: Noise-Resilient Detection of Neuronal Spikes by a Hopf-Bifurcation Device
summary: Detecting weak transient signals in noise is a persistent challenge in sensing, communication, and electrophysiology. Here, we demonstrate a physical weak-signal detector based on a semiconductor negative differential resistance (NDR) device operated near a Hopf bifurcation. A coherent input that persists over the response time of the dynamical system can drive a transition between quiescent and oscillatory states, whereas faster stochastic fluctuations are largely suppressed. This nonlinear transformation converts a weak analog threshold crossing into all-or-none voltage spikes and therefore provides asynchronous signal detection without a reference clock. Using a modulated photovoltaic signal, we detect a weak frequency component of 100 Hz as a demonstration, at an input signal-to-noise amplitude ratio as low as 1/500, and reliably recover it in the output spectrum. We then apply the same principle to neuronal multisite extracellular recordings. After standard band-pass filtering, the raw microelectrode signal is transformed by the NDR dynamics, enhancing the distinction between neuronal spikes and background fluctuations. The resulting detected spike times agree closely with those obtained using a traditional spike-detection pipeline. These results establish bifurcation-engineered NDR dynamics as a compact hardware approach to noise-resilient signal discrimination and event-based analog-to-digital conversion that will be useful for neuroprosthetic devices.

AI.tldr: The paper demonstrates a physical weak-signal detector using a semiconductor negative differential resistance (NDR) device operated near a Hopf bifurcation, which converts weak analog threshold crossings into all-or-none voltage spikes. It achieves detection at signal-to-noise amplitude ratios as low as 1/500 for a 100 Hz signal and successfully applies the same principle to neuronal spike detection from multisite extracellular recordings, establishing bifurcation-engineered NDR dynamics as a compact hardware approach for noise-resilient signal discrimination and event-based analog-to-digital conversion.
AI.motivation: Detecting weak transient signals buried in noise is a persistent challenge across sensing, communication, and electrophysiology applications. Existing approaches often rely on reference clocks or complex digital processing, motivating the need for a compact, asynchronous, physical detector that can discriminate coherent signals from stochastic noise without the overhead of traditional clocked systems.
AI.method: The authors exploit a semiconductor NDR device operated near a Hopf bifurcation. Coherent inputs persisting over the system response time drive a transition between quiescent and oscillatory states, while faster stochastic fluctuations are suppressed. This nonlinear transformation converts analog threshold crossings into all-or-none voltage spikes, enabling asynchronous signal detection without a reference clock. The approach was validated using a modulated photovoltaic signal (100 Hz detection at SNR amplitude ratio 1/500) and then applied to neuronal multisite extracellular recordings after standard band-pass filtering, transforming the microelectrode signal via NDR dynamics to enhance spike-background distinction.
AI.result: The detector reliably recovered a weak 100 Hz frequency component at an input signal-to-noise amplitude ratio as low as 1/500. In neuronal recordings, the NDR-transformed signals produced detected spike times that agreed closely with those from a traditional spike-detection pipeline, demonstrating enhanced discrimination between neuronal spikes and background fluctuations.
AI.conclusion: Bifurcation-engineered NDR dynamics provide a compact, hardware-based approach to noise-resilient signal discrimination and event-based analog-to-digital conversion, with practical potential for neuroprosthetic devices and other applications requiring asynchronous weak-signal detection.

title: What Photocurrent Versus Effective Voltage Tells Us About Charge Generation in Organic Solar Cells
summary: The photocurrent of an organic solar cell is routinely plotted against an effective voltage and used to extract an exciton dissociation probability, and through it a free-charge generation efficiency. The photocurrent measures neither. Using a drift-diffusion model in which free-charge generation is field independent and losses occur only by bimolecular recombination, we show that the apparent dissociation probability returned by this procedure lies well below unity even for complete dissociation. Across wide variations of carrier mobility and recombination strength it is a single-valued function of the fill factor and coincides with the short-circuit charge collection efficiency, reporting neither the generation yield nor anything about collection beyond what the fill factor already shows. Even for ideal transport the normalised photocurrent saturates below unity at an intensity-independent first-order limit set by recombination of photogenerated carriers with injected equilibrium charge. Applied to four organic solar cells whose generation efficiencies are known independently, the apparent dissociation probabilities track the short-circuit collection efficiency rather than the generation yield. We therefore suggest this construction not be used, particularly in the high-efficiency non-fullerene acceptor systems that are now state of the art.

AI.tldr: The paper shows that the common procedure of plotting photocurrent against effective voltage to extract an exciton dissociation probability is flawed: it measures neither dissociation nor free-charge generation efficiency. Using drift-diffusion modeling, the authors demonstrate the apparent dissociation probability actually equals the short-circuit charge collection efficiency and is a single-valued function of the fill factor. Even under ideal transport it saturates below unity due to recombination with injected equilibrium charge. They recommend abandoning this construction, especially for high-efficiency non-fullerene organic solar cells.
AI.motivation: A widely used experimental analysis extracts an "exciton dissociation probability" (and thereby free-charge generation efficiency) from photocurrent vs effective voltage curves in organic solar cells. The authors aim to test whether this procedure actually measures what it claims, given that photocurrent is a convolution of generation, transport, and recombination effects.
AI.method: The authors use a drift-diffusion model in which free-charge generation is explicitly field-independent and losses arise only from bimolecular recombination. They compute normalized photocurrent vs effective voltage curves across wide variations in carrier mobility and recombination strength, and compare the resulting apparent dissociation probabilities with both the modeled generation yield and the short-circuit charge collection efficiency. They also apply the analysis to four experimental organic solar cells whose true generation efficiencies are independently known.
AI.result: The apparent dissociation probability returned by the procedure lies well below unity even when dissociation is complete. It is a single-valued function of fill factor and coincides with the short-circuit charge collection efficiency—not the generation efficiency. Even for ideal transport, normalized photocurrent saturates below unity at an intensity-independent first-order limit set by recombination of photogenerated carriers with injected equilibrium charge. On real devices, the apparent probability tracks the short-circuit collection efficiency rather than the generation yield.
AI.conclusion: The photocurrent-vs-effective-voltage construction does not measure exciton dissociation or free-charge generation efficiency; it merely reports a quantity already captured by the fill factor. The authors recommend that this analysis method not be used, particularly in modern high-efficiency non-fullerene acceptor organic solar cells.

title: Thermoelectric properties of metal-semiconductor percolation composites
summary: We analyze thermoelectric response of composite materials comprising homogeneous semiconductor hosts with randomly distributed metallic inclusions. We demonstrate that the properties of such materials are strongly affected by the percolation transition (with background conductivity). We show that in vicinity of percolation threshold, the power factor and the thermoelectric figure of merit strongly depend on both the concentration and arrangement of inclusions. Finally, we identify promising regimes for enhancing the power factor in realistic composites.

AI.tldr: This paper analyzes thermoelectric properties of composite materials made of semiconductor hosts with randomly distributed metallic inclusions, showing that thermoelectric performance is strongly governed by percolation transitions and depends on inclusion concentration and arrangement near the percolation threshold, with promising regimes identified for power factor enhancement.
AI.motivation: To understand and predict how metallic inclusions distributed within semiconductor host materials affect thermoelectric performance, particularly through percolation effects.
AI.method: Analytical and/or computational analysis of thermoelectric response (power factor and figure of merit) in composite materials near the percolation threshold, examining dependence on inclusion concentration and spatial arrangement.
AI.result: Demonstrates that thermoelectric properties are strongly influenced by the percolation transition relative to background conductivity, with both power factor and thermoelectric figure of merit showing strong dependence on inclusion concentration and arrangement near the percolation threshold; identifies promising regimes for power factor enhancement in realistic composites.
AI.conclusion: Percolation-driven effects play a critical role in determining thermoelectric performance of semiconductor-metal composites, and tuning inclusion concentration and arrangement offers a viable pathway to enhance power factor in realistic material systems.

title: 4 MV/cm (010) $β$-Ga$_2$O$_3$ Heterojunction Diodes Realized by Low-Damage e-Beam NiO$_x$ Interlayers
summary: We report on the utilization of a low-damage e-beam NiO$_x$ deposition process to realize field-plated heterojunction diodes (FP-HJDs) on (010) $β$-Ga$_2$O$_3$ films with high critical breakdown field strengths beyond 4 MV/cm and power figure of merits (PFOM) of >1 GW/cm$^2$. Diodes were fabricated on a 2.67 $\times$ 10$^{16}$ cm$^{-3}$ intentionally doped 6.2 $μ$m thick epitaxial layer grown by metalorganic chemical vapor deposition (MOCVD) on a conductive Sn-doped $β$-Ga$_2$O$_3$ (010) substrate using TMGa, O$_2$, Ar carrier gas, and SiH$_4$ as the silicon dopant source. The mesa etched FP-HJD devices utilized a thin 7 nm e-beam NiO$_x$ interlayer before the sputtered NiO$_x$ layers to eliminate the effects of sputter-induced ion damage on the (010) epilayers. Current-Voltage measurements resulted in a forward current density of 700 A/cm$^2$ at 4 V, HJD ideality factor of 1.29, a V$_{bi}$ of 2 V, rectification ratio of 10$^{11}$, and a differential specific on resistance (R$_{on,sp}$) value of 2.36 m$Ω$ $\times$ cm$^2$. Breakdown of the (010) FP-HJDs was 1.64 kV, leading to a parallel plane electric field at breakdown (E$_{||,max}$) of 4.02 MV/cm and a PFOM of 1.14 GW/cm$^2$, which is a state-of-the-art result for diodes on MOCVD-grown (010) drift layers.

AI.tldr: This paper reports on low-damage e-beam NiOx-deposited field-plated heterojunction diodes (FP-HJDs) on (010) β-Ga2O3 MOCVD-grown epilayers, achieving critical breakdown field strengths >4 MV/cm, a PFOM of 1.14 GW/cm², and a breakdown voltage of 1.64 kV—a state-of-the-art result for such diodes.
AI.motivation: To achieve high critical breakdown field strengths and power figures of merit in β-Ga2O3 heterojunction diodes while mitigating sputter-induced ion damage on the (010) epilayer surface during NiOx deposition.
AI.method: A mesa-etched FP-HJD was fabricated on a 6.2 μm thick, 2.67×10¹⁶ cm⁻³ Si-doped (010) β-Ga2O3 drift layer grown by MOCVD on a conductive Sn-doped substrate. A thin 7 nm e-beam NiOx interlayer was deposited before sputtered NiOx layers to eliminate sputter-induced damage. Device performance was characterized via current-voltage measurements and breakdown testing.
AI.result: The device showed a forward current density of 700 A/cm² at 4 V, an ideality factor of 1.29, Vbi of 2 V, rectification ratio of 10¹¹, and Ron,sp of 2.36 mΩ·cm². Breakdown occurred at 1.64 kV, yielding a parallel-plane electric field of 4.02 MV/cm and a PFOM of 1.14 GW/cm²—a state-of-the-art result for diodes on MOCVD-grown (010) drift layers.
AI.conclusion: The e-beam NiOx interlayer strategy effectively mitigates sputter damage on (010) β-Ga2O3, enabling field-plated heterojunction diodes with record-high breakdown field (>4 MV/cm) and power figure of merit (>1 GW/cm²) on MOCVD-grown drift layers.

title: Reduced Precision Diffusion Synthetic Acceleration for S$_N$ Neutron Transport in LLNL's ARDRA using Hypre
comment: 10 pages, 7 figures, submitted to ANS M&C 2027
summary: Fast solution times in production discrete ordinates transport codes often require the use of diffusion synthetic acceleration (DSA). A good implementation of DSA will substantially reduce the number of iterations to converge the transport solution at the cost of solving a diffusion-like linear system at each iteration. Often fewer transport iterations will lead to smaller times to solution. Recent work has shown the promise of reduced precision preconditioning. Time and memory cost can be decreased as long as the reduced precision does not substantially degrade the convergence behavior of the higher precision linear system being solved. In this paper, we discuss the algorithmic implications of accelerating transport iterations in double precision (64 bit) while using a reduced precision (32 bit) DSA solve. We initially implement a stand alone code to investigate any theoretical limitations of reduced precision DSA in slabs. Then we implement reduced precision DSA in ARDRA, Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory's (LLNL) discrete ordinance neutral particle transport code, coupled with {\it hypre}, LLNL's scalable linear solver and multigrid methods library capable of mixed precision linear solves Then we solve various neutron transport problems of interest. We find that in most circumstances, DSA acceleration in reduced precision has little to no impact on the acceleration properties of DSA when used with source iteration in most circumstances. However, as tighter tolerances are required, reduced precision DSA may fail to successfully accelerate the transport solve and increase time to solution.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates using reduced precision (32-bit) Diffusion Synthetic Acceleration (DSA) to accelerate double precision (64-bit) transport solves in discrete ordinates codes. The authors implement reduced precision DSA first in a standalone slab code, then integrate it with ARDRA (LLNL's discrete ordinates transport code) coupled with the hypre solver library supporting mixed precision. Testing on neutron transport problems shows reduced precision DSA generally has little to no impact on acceleration properties with source iteration, but may fail to accelerate transport solves and increase time to solution when tighter tolerances are required.
AI.motivation: DSA is essential for fast convergence in discrete ordinates transport codes but requires solving a diffusion-like linear system at each iteration. Reduced precision preconditioning has shown promise in decreasing time and memory costs. The authors aim to explore whether using reduced precision (32-bit) for DSA solves can maintain convergence performance while offering computational savings when accelerating high-precision transport iterations.
AI.method: The authors first implement a standalone code to investigate theoretical limitations of reduced precision DSA in slab geometry. They then implement reduced precision DSA in ARDRA, LLNL's discrete ordinates neutral particle transport code, coupled with hypre, LLNL's scalable linear solver and multigrid methods library capable of mixed precision linear solves. Various neutron transport problems are solved to evaluate performance.
AI.result: In most circumstances, reduced precision DSA acceleration has little to no impact on the acceleration properties of DSA when used with source iteration. However, when tighter tolerances are required, reduced precision DSA may fail to successfully accelerate the transport solve, resulting in increased time to solution.
AI.conclusion: Reduced precision DSA is generally viable for most transport problems in terms of maintaining acceleration performance, but there is a tolerance threshold beyond which reduced precision degrades the ability to accelerate convergence and becomes counterproductive. Careful selection of tolerances is needed when applying reduced precision DSA in production transport codes.

title: Exact quantum spin liquids with topological order on maple-leaf and trellis lattices
summary: We construct spin models with bond-dependent anisotropic interactions on the penta-coordinated maple-leaf and trellis lattices, which yield exact $\mathbb{Z}_2$ quantum spin liquids akin to the Kitaev honeycomb model. We characterize the resulting ground states by their flux sectors, Chern numbers, and topological excitations. Using replica exchange quantum Monte Carlo simulations, we find that the gauge fluxes are ordered at sufficiently low temperatures such that every unit triangle has $\pm π/2$-flux, where the sign is uniform across the system, and every unit hexagon (square) has $0$-flux ($π$-flux) within the parameter space of interest. We map out the topological phase diagram for each model, which reveals parameter regimes hosting $\mathbb{Z}_2$ and Ising topological orders, and we derive an analytical expression for the mass term of the Majorana fermions, the vanishing of which indicates a transition between these phases. We further establish the correspondence between individual vortices (i.e., flux excitations) and two species of anyons in the dimer limit, overcoming the obstacle faced by degenerate perturbation theory in treating odd-length elementary plaquettes. Interestingly, we find that two dimer limits of the maple-leaf model with distinct assignments of anyon species can be smoothly connected to each other in the vortex-free sector, but they are separated by fermion-gap-closing transitions in certain two-vortex sectors.

AI.tldr: This paper constructs spin models with bond-dependent anisotropic interactions on maple-leaf and trellis lattices, yielding exact Z2 quantum spin liquids like the Kitaev honeycomb model. Using replica exchange QMC, the authors characterize ground states, map topological phase diagrams showing Z2 and Ising topological orders, derive Majorana mass terms, and establish vortex-anyon correspondences in the dimer limit.
AI.motivation: To extend the Kitaev honeycomb model's exact solvability to penta-coordinated lattices (maple-leaf and trellis), which contain odd-length elementary plaquettes. Such lattices present challenges for conventional degenerate perturbation theory when analyzing anyon-vortex correspondence, motivating an alternative approach to fully characterize the resulting quantum spin liquid phases.
AI.method: The authors construct spin models with bond-dependent anisotropic interactions on maple-leaf and trellis lattices. They employ replica exchange quantum Monte Carlo to study flux ordering at low temperatures, compute Chern numbers and flux sectors for ground-state characterization, derive analytical expressions for Majorana fermion mass terms, and establish vortex-anyon correspondence via the dimer limit to overcome obstacles from odd-length elementary plaquettes in degenerate perturbation theory.
AI.result: Gauge fluxes order at low temperatures such that every unit triangle has ±π/2-flux with a uniform sign, every unit hexagon has 0-flux, and every unit square has π-flux in the parameter range of interest. Topological phase diagrams were mapped out revealing regimes with Z2 and Ising topological orders. Two dimer limits of the maple-leaf model with distinct anyon species assignments connect smoothly in the vortex-free sector but are separated by fermion-gap-closing transitions in certain two-vortex sectors.
AI.conclusion: The work demonstrates that exact Z2 quantum spin liquids can be realized on penta-coordinated lattices, generalizes Kitaev-type physics beyond honeycomb-like geometries, and provides a framework (dimer-limit analysis) to handle odd-length plaquettes that evade standard degenerate perturbation theory.

title: Orientation selection and superconducting properties of epitaxial Al on ferromagnetic semiconductor (In,Fe)As
summary: Superconductor/ferromagnet heterostructures provide a versatile platform for exploring spin-dependent superconducting phenomena arising from interfacial proximity effects. In this article, we investigate the structural and superconducting properties of Al thin films grown in situ by molecular beam epitaxy on strained Fe-doped ferromagnetic semiconductor (FMS) (In,Fe)As layers. X-ray diffraction and transmission electron microscopy reveal the epitaxial growth of single-crystalline Al layers, with the growth orientation changing from (110) to (111) as the in-plane lattice constant of (In,Fe)As increases. The superconducting critical temperature of Al varies systematically with the film surface morphology and grain size. In addition, the critical magnetic field of Al exhibits an anomalous decrease below 0.5 K, possibly reflecting magnetic coupling to the underlying FMS (In,Fe)As layer. These findings provide a guideline for material design of epitaxial Al/(In,Fe)As heterostructures, which may serve as a promising platform for investigating proximity-induced superconducting and magnetic phenomena in semiconductor-based hybrid quantum devices.

AI.tldr: This paper studies epitaxial Al thin films grown by MBE on strain-tuned ferromagnetic semiconductor (In,Fe)As layers, showing orientation-dependent growth (Al(110) to Al(111)), systematic variation of superconducting critical temperature with morphology/grain size, and an anomalous suppression of the critical magnetic field below 0.5 K attributed to magnetic coupling with the underlying FMS layer. These results offer design guidelines for Al/(In,Fe)As heterostructures for proximity-induced superconducting phenomena in hybrid quantum devices.
AI.motivation: To explore spin-dependent superconducting phenomena from interfacial proximity effects by growing epitaxial superconducting Al films on a ferromagnetic semiconductor platform, and to establish structure-property relationships that guide the design of semiconductor-based hybrid quantum devices.
AI.method: Al thin films were grown in situ by molecular beam epitaxy on strained Fe-doped ferromagnetic semiconductor (In,Fe)As layers. Structural characterization employed X-ray diffraction and transmission electron microscopy to determine crystallographic orientation and epitaxial quality. Superconducting properties (critical temperature and critical magnetic field) were measured, correlating with film surface morphology, grain size, and lattice mismatch.
AI.result: Single-crystalline epitaxial Al films were achieved with growth orientation transitioning from (110) to (111) as the in-plane lattice constant of (In,Fe)As increased. The superconducting critical temperature varied systematically with surface morphology and grain size. An anomalous decrease in critical magnetic field was observed below 0.5 K, possibly indicating magnetic coupling between the Al layer and the underlying FMS layer.
AI.conclusion: The findings provide material design guidelines for epitaxial Al/(In,Fe)As heterostructures, which represent a promising platform for investigating proximity-induced superconducting and magnetic phenomena in semiconductor-based hybrid quantum devices.

title: Fukui-Kawakami chains: spectrum and hidden $\mathfrak{gl}(1|1)$-symmetry
summary:
Fukui and Kawakami showed that the trigonometric Haldane--Shastry (HS) spin chain can be deformed by introducing twisted boundary conditions. In this work we revisit the resulting twisted HS chains, which we call Fukui--Kawakami (FK) chains.
  We analyse their spectra in dependence of the twist parameter, utilising a direct connection with the (untwisted) HS chain. This allows us to explain why part of the spectrum can be described by Fukui and Kawakami's twisted Bethe equations, and can be constructed from Yangian highest weight states. These states can be labelled by combinatorial data called `motifs', as in the HS chain, which cover some of the (deformed) descendants. We furthermore show that there are other descendants which do not follow from these Bethe equations, but whose energy can be described as a sum of two single-particle energies, suggesting additional hidden symmetries.
  We then focus on the special case of antiperiodic boundary conditions, and show that this chain coincides with the `minimally polarised' long-range model recently introduced by Basu-Mallick, Finkel, and González-López. Remarkably, this connection implies that the antiperiodic chain has a hidden $\mathfrak{gl}(1|1)$-symmetry, which we use to relate the HS motifs to their `supersymmetric' $\mathfrak{gl}(1|1)$ counterparts.

AI.tldr: This paper revisits the Fukui-Kawakami (FK) chain, a twisted trigonometric Haldane-Shastry spin chain, analyzing its spectrum as a function of the twist parameter via its connection to the untwisted HS chain. The authors explain why part of the spectrum follows from twisted Bethe equations constructible from Yangian highest weight states labelled by motifs, while other descendants (with energies as sums of two single-particle terms) suggest hidden symmetries. They further show that in the antiperiodic case the chain matches the 'minimally polarised' long-range model of Basu-Mallick, Finkel, and González-López, revealing a hidden gl(1|1) symmetry linking HS motifs to their supersymmetric counterparts.
AI.motivation: To understand the spectrum and algebraic/structural properties of twisted Haldane-Shastry chains (Fukui-Kawakami chains) by leveraging their relationship with the untwisted HS chain, and to uncover hidden symmetries, particularly in the antiperiodic case where the chain connects to a supersymmetric long-range model.
AI.method: The authors exploit a direct connection between twisted FK chains and the untwisted HS chain to analyse the twist-parameter dependence of the spectrum. They utilise twisted Bethe ansatz equations and Yangian highest weight representations, labelling states by combinatorial motifs. For the antiperiodic boundary condition, they identify the chain with the 'minimally polarised' long-range model, enabling the use of a hidden gl(1|1) algebra to map HS motifs to supersymmetric gl(1|1) counterparts.
AI.result: Part of the FK spectrum is exactly captured by twisted Bethe equations derived from Yangian highest weight states labelled by motifs. However, additional descendants exist that do not obey these Bethe equations but have energies expressible as sums of two single-particle energies, hinting at extra hidden symmetries. The antiperiodic FK chain is shown to coincide with the minimally polarised long-range model, which possesses a hidden gl(1|1) symmetry used to relate HS motifs to their supersymmetric analogues.
AI.conclusion: The FK chains exhibit a richer structure than previously understood: while twisted Bethe equations describe a substantial subset of the spectrum tied to Yangian highest weight motifs, the existence of extra descendants indicates further hidden symmetries. The antiperiodic case provides a concrete realisation with a hidden gl(1|1) supersymmetry, establishing a novel correspondence between the HS chain's combinatorial data and supersymmetric quantum integrable models.

title: Enhanced Multifractality Induced by Non-Hermitian Disorder in Quantum Percolation
summary: We investigate the interplay between geometric dilution and non-Hermitian disorder in the two-dimensional quantum site-percolation model. Non-Hermiticity is introduced through random imaginary on-site potentials, representing spatially uncorrelated gain and loss, while the hopping amplitudes remain reciprocal. By combining complex level-spacing statistics, participation entropy, and multifractal analysis, we characterize the localization properties of the eigenstates as functions of the disorder and the non-Hermiticity strength. Our finite-size scaling results show that non-Hermitian disorder shifts the quantum percolation threshold ($p_q$) toward larger occupation probabilities. Consequently, the fully delocalized phase is progressively suppressed and disappears at sufficiently strong disorder. This suppression is not a simple consequence of adding on-site disorder of a given strength, but is specifically enhanced by its imaginary character, as an equally strong real (Hermitian) on-site potential produces a weaker shift of $p_q$. Nevertheless, the intermediate region between the classical ($p_c$) and quantum percolation thresholds presents a genuine multifractal critical phase, while the localization-length exponent $ν$ remains the same, relative to its Hermitian value. Altogether, our results demonstrate that random gain and loss enhance the multifractal regime while preserving the universality class of the quantum percolation transition.

AI.tldr: This paper studies how non-Hermitian disorder (random imaginary on-site potentials) affects the two-dimensional quantum site-percolation model. Using complex level-spacing statistics, participation entropy, and multifractal analysis, the authors find that non-Hermitian disorder shifts the quantum percolation threshold toward larger occupation probabilities, eventually suppressing the fully delocalized phase. The intermediate region between classical and quantum thresholds remains a genuine multifractal critical phase, and the localization-length exponent is unchanged from its Hermitian value, indicating the universality class is preserved.
AI.motivation: To understand how geometric dilution (percolation) and non-Hermitian disorder (random gain and loss) interplay in controlling the localization properties of eigenstates in a two-dimensional quantum system, and to determine whether non-Hermiticity changes the nature of the quantum percolation transition.
AI.method: The model is a two-dimensional quantum site-percolation system with reciprocal hopping, where non-Hermiticity is introduced via random imaginary on-site potentials representing uncorrelated gain and loss. The authors employ three complementary diagnostics: complex level-spacing statistics, participation entropy, and multifractal analysis, combined with finite-size scaling to characterize eigenstate localization as functions of disorder and non-Hermiticity strength.
AI.result: Non-Hermitian disorder shifts the quantum percolation threshold ($p_q$) toward larger occupation probabilities, suppressing and eventually eliminating the fully delocalized phase at sufficiently strong disorder. The suppression is specifically due to the imaginary character of the disorder—an equally strong real (Hermitian) on-site potential produces a weaker shift. A genuine multifractal critical phase persists in the region between the classical ($p_c$) and quantum ($p_q$) thresholds, and the localization-length exponent $ν$ remains identical to its Hermitian value.
AI.conclusion: Random gain and loss enhance the multifractal regime in the quantum site-percolation model while preserving the universality class of the quantum percolation transition, as evidenced by the unchanged localization-length exponent.

title: Learning multistate kinetics with a variational multistate committor network
summary: The long-time dynamics of complex molecular systems often involves rare transitions across networks of metastable states. Building on transition-path theory, which provides a rigorous framework for describing rare transitions between two metastable states, we introduce the variational multistate committor network (VMCN), a neural framework that learns the probabilities of reaching each metastable state directly from molecular simulation data. From this representation, VMCN identifies state-specific commitment, candidate transition regions and committor-consistent pathways between state pairs, and an effective kinetic network characterized by transition rates. The model is trained using finite time-lag trajectory data together with boundary conditions defined on conservative state cores. Applications to a triple-well potential, trialanine isomerization, and the $c$--ring rotation in the V$_{\rm o}$ domain of a vacuolar ATPase show that VMCN recovers metastable organization, provides committor-consistent descriptions of transition mechanisms, and estimates state-to-state kinetics. VMCN further provides diagnostics for incomplete state decompositions and enables adaptive exploration of candidate metastable states and their connecting regions. By integrating VMCN with generative committor-guided path sampling (Gen-COMPAS) for chignolin, we start from two end point structures, identify a misfolded state and a candidate folding intermediate, and we direct subsequent sampling toward the resulting multistate transition network.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces VMCN, a neural framework based on transition-path theory that learns committor probabilities to all metastable states directly from molecular simulation data, enabling identification of state-specific commitment, transition regions, pathways, and kinetic rates. Applications to model potentials, peptides, and a membrane protein complex validate its ability to recover metastable organization and kinetics, with additional integration to generative path sampling enabling adaptive exploration of metastable networks.
AI.motivation: Rare transitions across networks of metastable states govern long-time dynamics of complex molecular systems, yet existing methods (e.g., pairwise transition-path theory) are limited to two-state descriptions and cannot naturally handle multistate networks with interconnected metastable states.
AI.method: VMCN extends transition-path theory to the multistate setting by training a neural network to learn the probability of reaching each metastable state from finite time-lag trajectory data, with boundary conditions defined on conservative state cores. This representation yields state commitment probabilities, transition regions, committor-consistent pathways, and an effective kinetic network with transition rates. It is further coupled with generative committor-guided path sampling (Gen-COMPAS) for adaptive exploration.
AI.result: Applications to a triple-well potential, trialanine isomerization, and the c-ring rotation in the Vo domain of vacuolar ATPase show that VMCN recovers metastable organization, provides committor-consistent transition mechanisms, and estimates state-to-state kinetics. In the chignolin case, VMCN identified a misfolded state and candidate folding intermediate when initialized from only two end-point structures.
AI.conclusion: VMCN provides a general framework for multistate rare-event analysis with built-in diagnostics for incomplete state decompositions, enabling adaptive exploration of metastable states and their connecting regions, thereby advancing the study of complex molecular networks.

title: Analytical model for polarization transfer during gas-phase collision events in spin-exchange optical pumping: Spin-$\frac{1}{2}$ $^{129}$Xe versus spin-$\frac{3}{2}$ $^{131}$Xe
summary: Spin-exchange optical pumping (SEOP) is a method for producing spin-hyperpolarized noble gas nuclei, such as 129Xe and 131Xe, which are used in various magnetic resonance applications from fundamental physics to quantum sensing and medical imaging. In SEOP, optically polarized alkali-metal atoms transfer their spin polarization to the noble gas nuclei in gas-phase collision events via the hyperfine coupling (HFC) between the alkali valence electron and the noble gas nucleus. While the polarization transfer physics of spin $I = 1/2$ nuclei, such as 129Xe, is relatively well understood, that of spin $I > 1/2$ nuclei, such as 131Xe ($I = 3/2$), has been far less studied, and no rigorous theoretical model has been presented to date. To this end, we derive a simple analytical model for the upper limit, neglecting relaxation, of the SEOP polarization transfer, applicable to noble gases with arbitrary nuclear spin. Analytical evaluation of the Baker-Campbell-Hausdorff expansion for the time evolution of the spin density operator $\hatρ(t)$ reveals that only even-order terms in the HFC contribute to the polarization transfer, with the leading-order quadratic term being the most significant. We obtain a result similar to that derived for the spin-exchange cross section by Herman [Phys. Rev. 137, A 1062 (1965)], but in a more general framework for the time evolution of $\hatρ(t)$ that is also more familiar to magnetic resonance researchers. The model is applied to understand the difference in the polarization transfer efficiency between 129Xe and 131Xe, yielding results in agreement with previous experiments. We also validate the model by comparison to detailed numerical multiscale simulations of the SEOP process, where full quantum-chemically computed spin Hamiltonians sampled from molecular dynamics simulations of the gas-phase collision events are used to propagate the spin dynamics.

AI.tldr: The paper derives a simple analytical model for the upper limit (neglecting relaxation) of spin-exchange optical pumping (SEOP) polarization transfer applicable to noble gases with arbitrary nuclear spin, using the Baker-Campbell-Hausdorff expansion for the time evolution of the spin density operator. The model reveals only even-order HFC terms contribute to polarization transfer, is validated against experiments for 129Xe versus 131Xe, and agrees with detailed numerical multiscale simulations using quantum-chemically computed spin Hamiltonians.
AI.motivation: While SEOP polarization transfer physics for spin I=1/2 nuclei like 129Xe is well understood, that for spin I>1/2 nuclei like 131Xe (I=3/2) has been far less studied, and no rigorous theoretical model has been presented to date.
AI.method: The authors derive a simple analytical model for the upper limit (neglecting relaxation) of SEOP polarization transfer applicable to noble gases with arbitrary nuclear spin, based on analytical evaluation of the Baker-Campbell-Hausdorff expansion for the time evolution of the spin density operator ρ̂(t). They identify that only even-order terms in the hyperfine coupling contribute to polarization transfer, with the leading-order quadratic term being most significant. They compare with Herman's spin-exchange cross section result (1965) in a more general framework, and validate the model against experiments and detailed numerical multiscale simulations using quantum-chemical spin Hamiltonians sampled from molecular dynamics simulations of gas-phase collisions.
AI.result: The model yields results in agreement with previous experiments explaining the difference in polarization transfer efficiency between 129Xe and 131Xe, and is validated by comparison to detailed numerical multiscale simulations of the SEOP process.
AI.conclusion: The authors provide a rigorous and general analytical framework for SEOP polarization transfer that works for arbitrary nuclear spin, extending beyond the well-studied spin I=1/2 case, with confirmed agreement between theory, experiment, and full numerical multiscale simulation.

title: The influence of quantum geometry on the phase boundary and collective excitations of electron liquids and crystals
summary: Recent experiments on multilayer graphene systems have reinvigorated the study of electron crystallization, now with the inclusion of quantum geometry. In this work, we apply time-dependent Hartree-Fock (TDHF) to the $λ$-jellium model to analyze the impact that quantum geometry has on the electronic liquid--crystal phase diagram and how it modifies the collective modes and responses of the liquid and crystal phases. In agreement with recent results utilizing neural quantum states, we find that quantum geometry favours electron crystallization, shifting the transition to higher densities. We also study the instabilities revealed by TDHF in the Fermi liquid ground state at low densities, providing insight into the fluctuations driving the crystallization transition. We further find that quantum geometry reduces the dispersion of the plasmon mode and suppresses Friedel oscillations deep in the liquid phase. Resolving the density response in terms of individual orbitals, we find that this suppression is caused by spectral weight transfer to an out-of-phase inter-orbital mode. Finally, we show that an analogous mode that emerges in the crystal phase corresponds to the breathing mode of an emergent real-space pseudospin skyrmion lattice.

AI.tldr: The paper applies time-dependent Hartree-Fock theory to the λ-jellium model of multilayer graphene to study how quantum geometry affects the electronic liquid-crystal phase diagram and collective excitations. Quantum geometry favors crystallization, reduces plasmon dispersion, suppresses Friedel oscillations via spectral weight transfer to an inter-orbital mode, and yields an analogous breathing mode in the crystal phase tied to a pseudospin skyrmion lattice.
AI.motivation: Recent experiments on multilayer graphene have revived interest in electron crystallization, now including effects of quantum geometry. The authors aim to understand how quantum geometry modifies the liquid-crystal phase diagram and the collective modes/responses of both phases.
AI.method: Time-dependent Hartree-Fock (TDHF) applied to the λ-jellium model of multilayer graphene, with analysis of ground-state instabilities, collective modes, and density response resolved in terms of individual orbitals.
AI.result: Quantum geometry favors electron crystallization (transition shifts to higher densities), consistent with neural quantum state results. TDHF reveals instabilities in the Fermi liquid at low densities. Quantum geometry reduces plasmon dispersion and suppresses Friedel oscillations via spectral weight transfer to an out-of-phase inter-orbital mode. An analogous mode in the crystal phase corresponds to the breathing mode of a real-space pseudospin skyrmion lattice.
AI.conclusion: Quantum geometry plays a significant role in shaping both the phase diagram and collective dynamics of electron systems in multilayer graphene, driving crystallization and modifying spectral responses through geometric effects encoded in orbital/inter-orbital modes and skyrmion-like lattice excitations.

title: Reproducible capillary fluctuation analysis of solid-liquid interfaces for stiffness and anisotropy calculations
summary: The capillary fluctuation method (CFM) is widely used to compute solid--liquid interfacial properties from atomistic simulations, but its accuracy depends on choices in interface construction, wave-vector selection, sampling, and simulation geometry. Here, we develop a diagnostics-driven workflow for reproducible CFM calculations using pure Al as a representative system. Employing both ribbon models and thick two-dimensional references, we show that apparent linearity of the fluctuation spectrum alone does not ensure reliable stiffness or anisotropy estimates. Instead, a reliable CFM analysis requires a fitting window consistent with both temporal sampling and continuum capillary-wave assumptions, systematic sensitivity tests of the interface identification procedure, explicit propagation of replica variability, and independent verification of model-thickness convergence. We further propose a practical thickness-selection rule based on coexistence-temperature consistency, which enables finite-size effects to be controlled while retaining the substantial computational efficiency of ribbon geometries. By making the main sources of uncertainty explicit and diagnosable, the proposed workflow improves the reliability of the CFM as a quantitative tool and provides a foundation for its broader application to complex solid--liquid interfaces.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a diagnostics-driven workflow for reproducible capillary fluctuation method (CFM) calculations of solid-liquid interfacial properties, using pure Al as a test system. It shows that apparent spectral linearity is insufficient for reliability and introduces concrete guidelines—fitting-window selection, sensitivity tests, replica-variability propagation, and thickness-convergence checks—plus a coexistence-temperature-based thickness-rule that preserves ribbon-geometry efficiency while controlling finite-size effects.
AI.motivation: CFM accuracy depends on numerous subjective choices (interface construction, wave-vector selection, sampling, simulation geometry), and apparent linearity of the fluctuation spectrum does not guarantee reliable stiffness or anisotropy estimates, so a systematic, diagnostic-driven framework is needed.
AI.method: The authors develop a workflow using pure Al, comparing ribbon models with thick two-dimensional references. They require a fitting window consistent with temporal sampling and continuum capillary-wave assumptions, run systematic sensitivity tests of interface identification, propagate replica variability explicitly, and verify model-thickness convergence. They also propose a thickness-selection rule grounded in coexistence-temperature consistency.
AI.result: The workflow makes principal uncertainty sources explicit and diagnosable, improves CFM reliability as a quantitative tool, and enables finite-size effects to be controlled while maintaining the computational efficiency of ribbon geometries.
AI.conclusion: The proposed diagnostic workflow improves reproducibility and reliability of CFM calculations and establishes a foundation for extending the method to more complex solid-liquid interfaces.

title: Three-Electrode TiO2 + rGO Cells: Classical Controls and Interpretation within a Quantum-Discord Framework
comment: 31 pages, 7 figures; Supplementary Material: 9 pages, 4 figures
summary: In three-electrode electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS), the impedance/capacitance response of the working electrode (WE) is measured relative to the reference electrode (RE), whereas the current required by potentiostatic control flows between the WE and the counter electrode (CE). Under classical three-electrode operation, the measured WE-RE response should therefore be independent of the properties of the electrode used as the CE, provided that conventional electrochemical and instrumental artifacts are negligible. Here, we test this expectation in cells containing nanostructured electrodes TiO2 + rGO and examine the results within a framework motivated by quantum discord to describe effective interelectrode correlations. We used dummy-cell measurements, a two-electrode bar-bar control, comparisons between Pt and bar CEs, a dummy circuit introduced into the CE branch, and CE ensemble comparisons to distinguish additive circuit behavior from CE-dependent behavior specific to the three-electrode configuration. In these experiments, the measured three-electrode capacitance response depends on CE, an effect that is not reproduced by the dummy-circuit controls examined. These findings identify a macroscopic CE-dependent capacitance response that departs from the tested classical expectation and is compatible with an effective interelectrode-correlation framework motivated by quantum discord, although the capacitance evidence alone does not constitute a direct measurement of quantum discord.
