The authors map out the quantum phase diagram as a function of single-ion anisotropy and field, identifying dipolar and quadrupolar spin supersolids (with coexisting U(1) symmetry breaking and translational symmetry breaking), an up-up-down phase at intermediate fields, and quadrupolar/dipolar spin superfluids at high fields. Dynamic spin structure factors reveal gapless Goldstone modes and roton-like minima accessible to neutron scattering. Results are relevant to triangular antiferromagnets like Na2BaNi(PO4)2 and K2Ni(SeO3)2.
AI.motivation: To understand the interplay between frustration, single-ion anisotropy, and Zeeman interactions in driving distinct spin supersolid phases in spin-1 triangular-lattice systems, which remain poorly understood compared to spin-1/2 counterparts and are experimentally relevant to compounds like Na2BaNi(PO4)2 and K2Ni(SeO3)2.
AI.method: Density Matrix Renormalization Group (DMRG) numerical simulations on the spin-1 antiferromagnetic Heisenberg model on the triangular lattice with out-of-plane magnetic field and single-ion anisotropy D_z. Phase boundaries and characters are determined via order parameters and spin superfluid stiffness across various system sizes, supplemented by dynamical spin structure factor calculations.
AI.result: The phase diagram reveals: (a) at zero field, a dipolar 'Y-type' spin supersolid persisting down to D_z=0 and a quadrupolar spin supersolid at large D_z; (b) an up-up-down phase dominating intermediate fields; (c) at high fields, a quadrupolar spin superfluid for large D_z and a dipolar 'V-type' spin supersolid for small D_z. Dynamical structure factors show characteristic gapless Goldstone modes and roton-like minima distinguishing each phase.
AI.conclusion: The work provides a comprehensive theoretical phase diagram of spin-1 triangular-lattice antiferromagnets under field and anisotropy, showing how frustration, anisotropy, and Zeeman coupling jointly stabilize distinct dipolar and quadrupolar supersolid/superfluid phases. These phases carry characteristic spectral signatures observable in inelastic neutron scattering, offering testable predictions for candidate materials.

title: Dynamical Reduction of Two Series Josephson Junctions to a Synthetic High-Transparency Josephson Element
comment: 5 pages, 2 figures. Submitted as a WOLTE17 contribution for consideration in the IEEE Trans. Appl. Supercond. Special Issue
summary: Two conventional Josephson junctions connected in series can reproduce, in the static limit in which the currents through the capacitive and resistive channels are negligible, the current-phase relation of a single effective weak link with tunable transparency. Therefore, the two-junction series can be treated as a single synthetic high-transparency element. Here, we investigate to what extent this mapping remains valid under finite-frequency drive and retaining the junctions' resistive and capacitive terms. The full resistively and capacitively shunted junction equations are compared with an effective synthetic element with tunable transparency that retains the synthetic tunable-transparency current-phase relation together with effective capacitive and dissipative terms, thus reducing the two second order degree of freedom system to a single second order degree of freedom. The resulting single-element dynamics is compared with the complete two-junction system under ac excitation. The agreement is quantified through a normalized root-mean-square error between the full and effective voltage waveforms. A broad low-error region is found at low drive frequency, while pronounced deviations emerge as the drive frequency approaches the relevant plasma-frequency scale and at larger drive amplitudes. The results provide a quantitative dynamical criterion for using the reduced single-element description of a synthetic high-transparency Josephson element in superconducting circuits.

AI.tldr: The paper investigates whether two series-connected Josephson junctions can be accurately modeled as a single synthetic high-transparency Josephson element under finite-frequency drive. By comparing full resistively and capacitively shunted junction equations with an effective single-element description, the authors find broad agreement at low drive frequencies but significant deviations approaching plasma-frequency scales and at larger amplitudes, providing a quantitative criterion for when the reduced model is valid.
AI.motivation: Two Josephson junctions in series can reproduce the static current-phase relation of a single effective weak link with tunable transparency, enabling it to be treated as one synthetic high-transparency element. However, the validity of this mapping under non-static (finite-frequency) conditions, including resistive and capacitive terms, was previously unclear. The paper aims to establish the dynamical regime of validity for this reduced description.
AI.method: The full resistively and capacitively shunted junction (RCSJ) equations for two series junctions are compared against an effective synthetic element that retains the tunable-transparency current-phase relation together with effective capacitive and dissipative terms, reducing a two second-order degree-of-freedom system to a single second-order degree of freedom. Agreement between the complete two-junction system and the effective single-element dynamics under ac excitation is quantified via normalized root-mean-square error between the full and effective voltage waveforms.

AI.conclusion: The results provide a quantitative dynamical criterion for when the reduced single-element description of a synthetic high-transparency Josephson element is valid in superconducting circuits, showing it is justified at sufficiently low drive frequencies but breaks down near plasma-frequency scales and at higher drive amplitudes.

title: Excitation caging in a vertex-frustrated quasiperiodic Einstein artificial spin ice
comment: Main text 8 pages and 4 figures, Methods 3 pages, Supplementary material 10 pages
summary: Naturally occurring bulk quasicrystals are rare, and magnetic instances are rarer still, with chemical constraints typically permitting the synthesis of approximants rather than true quasicrystalline magnets. Here, we present an artificial spin ice based on a recently discovered Einstein lattice, the Hat tiling, which is built from the first known shape - the hat - that tiles the plane only aperiodically. The Einstein artificial spin ice has long-range structural order with no translational symmetry, and low-connectivity vertices with well-defined local ground states and excitations. Together, these properties provide a model two-dimensional quasicrystalline magnet, with magnetic correlations that we probe with magnetic force microscopy and parallel-tempered Monte Carlo simulations. We identify a two-stage partial ordering process, driven by the competition between two possible positions for magnetic excitations. This competition is resolved in the ground-state manifold, where exactly one magnetic excitation is caged on each antihat, yet the manifold remains macroscopically degenerate. This yields an unusual type of medium-range order, where the underlying quasiperiodic long-range order is randomly modulated by a strictly constrained disorder. Our findings establish the Einstein artificial spin ice as a blueprint for understanding quasicrystalline magnetism, demonstrating how quasiperiodic monotile geometries can be exploited to engineer unconventional magnetic phases with no direct equivalent in periodic systems.

This Einstein artificial spin ice serves as a model two-dimensional quasicrystalline magnet with long-range structural order but no translational symmetry. Using magnetic force microscopy and parallel-tempered Monte Carlo simulations, they find a two-stage partial ordering process driven by competition between two positions for magnetic excitations, resulting in a macroscopically degenerate ground-state manifold with caged excitations and an unusual medium-range order where quasiperiodic long-range order is randomly modulated by constrained disorder.
AI.motivation: Bulk quasicrystals with magnetic properties are extremely rare and chemically constrained, typically only permitting approximant synthesis. The authors aim to create a true quasicrystalline magnetic system using artificial spin ice to overcome these chemical constraints.
AI.method: The authors fabricated an artificial spin ice (ASI) based on the Hat tiling—an Einstein lattice made from the first known monotile that tiles only aperiodically—and studied its magnetic correlations using magnetic force microscopy and parallel-tempered Monte Carlo simulations.
AI.result: They identified a two-stage partial ordering process driven by competition between two possible positions for magnetic excitations. In the ground-state manifold, exactly one magnetic excitation is caged on each antihat, yet the manifold remains macroscopically degenerate, yielding an unusual medium-range order with randomly modulated quasiperiodic long-range order.
AI.conclusion: The Einstein artificial spin ice establishes a blueprint for quasicrystalline magnetism, demonstrating how quasiperiodic monotile geometries can be exploited to engineer unconventional magnetic phases with no direct equivalents in periodic systems.

title: Structural tuning of reduced exciton mass in layered HOIP compounds: Causation vs. correlation
comment: 27 pages, 14 figures. For associated SI information, see DOI 10.5281/zenodo.22261753
summary: Reduced exciton mass ($μ$) was recently reported to correlate strongly with a framework distortion in a series of nine single-layer (2D) metal-halide perovskite (HOIP) compounds. Specifically, $μ$ was observed to increase in tandem with an alternating PbI4 octahedral tilt about an in-plane axis. In this work, we use group representation theory to decompose the observed framework distortions into displacive symmetry modes of a common high-symmetry parent framework. We find that all nine distorted frameworks involve linear combinations of the same six symmetry modes, which have been reported to contribute to the framework distortions of a wide range of HOIP compounds. We show that these modes have highly correlated impacts on the band structure. To differentiate causation from correlation, we vary the amplitude of each mode independently and use density-functional theory to determine the resulting electronic band structures, from which $μ$ is extracted. We find that bond-transverse displacements of the equatorial halide atoms increase $μ$, while bond-transverse displacements of the apical halide atoms decrease it. Bond-axis displacements appear to have little or no effect on $μ$. Our results demonstrate three new structure-property relationships, revealing a promising new avenue for exciton engineering in layered perovskite materials.

AI.tldr: The study decomposes framework distortions in nine 2D metal-halide perovskites into six symmetry modes and uses DFT to systematically vary each mode, finding that bond-transverse equatorial halide displacements increase exciton mass while bond-transverse apical halide displacements decrease it, with bond-axis displacements having little effect.
AI.motivation: Recent experiments showed a strong correlation between reduced exciton mass and framework distortion (octahedral tilt) in layered perovskites, but correlation alone cannot establish causation. The authors aim to differentiate which specific distortion modes actually control exciton mass.
AI.method: Group representation theory is used to decompose the observed framework distortions of nine single-layer metal-halide perovskites into displacive symmetry modes of a common high-symmetry parent framework. The amplitude of each mode is then varied independently, and density-functional theory (DFT) is used to compute electronic band structures from which reduced exciton mass is extracted.

Independent mode variation reveals that bond-transverse displacements of equatorial halide atoms increase reduced exciton mass, bond-transverse displacements of apical halide atoms decrease it, and bond-axis displacements have little or no effect.
AI.conclusion: Three new structure-property relationships are demonstrated, providing a promising new avenue for exciton engineering in layered perovskite materials by selectively tuning specific phonon-like symmetry modes.

title: Symmetry-protected triplet Weyl complexes
summary: The Nielsen-Ninomiya theorem dictates that Weyl nodes must appear in pairs of opposite chirality to preserve global charge neutrality. However, in crystals, specific crystalline symmetries can stabilize multi-Weyl nodes, circumventing this pairwise constraint and enabling compensated Weyl complexes with mixed chiral charges. The minimal configuration of this type is a triplet Weyl complex (TWC), comprising exactly three Weyl nodes. Here, we systematically investigate the symmetry conditions required to realize TWCs. By screening all 1651 magnetic space groups (MSGs) in both spinless and spinful systems, we establish that: (i) Only TWCs with charge magnitudes of $\{1,1,2\}$ and $\{1,2,3\}$ are permitted; (ii) the $\{1,1,2\}$ configuration can be realized in 166 spinless MSGs and 70 spinful MSGs; and (iii) the $\{1,2,3\}$-TWCs, which has not been reported before, can occur in 10 MSGs for both spinless and spinful cases. We explicitly demonstrate the existence of $\{1,2,3\}$-TWC in a tight-binding model. Furthermore, we present the first electronic realization of $\{1,1,2\}$-TWC topological semimetal state in the chiral carbon allotrope DZQH-C$_{36}$, in which the three Weyl nodes form a collinear configuration, leading to a characteristic ``S''-shaped surface Fermi arc pattern. Our findings uncover novel topological states featuring mixed chiral charges and provide guidance for exploring their physics in concrete material systems.

The {1,1,2}-TWC occurs in 166 spinless and 70 spinful MSGs, while the previously unreported {1,2,3}-TWC appears in 10 MSGs. The authors demonstrate {1,2,3}-TWC in a tight-binding model and present the first electronic realization of {1,1,2}-TWC in the chiral carbon allotrope DZQH-C36, exhibiting an S-shaped surface Fermi arc pattern.
AI.motivation: While the Nielsen-Ninomiya theorem generally requires Weyl nodes to appear in pairs of opposite chirality, crystalline symmetries can stabilize multi-Weyl nodes and enable compensated Weyl complexes with mixed chiral charges. The minimal such configuration—a triplet Weyl complex (TWC) with exactly three Weyl nodes—has not been systematically characterized, motivating a comprehensive symmetry-based classification to discover novel topological states.
AI.method: The authors screen all 1651 magnetic space groups (MSGs) for both spinless and spinful systems to identify which crystallographic symmetries can stabilize TWCs. They classify allowed charge configurations and enumerate MSGs supporting each type. They construct a tight-binding model to verify the existence of the {1,2,3}-TWC and perform electronic structure calculations to realize the {1,1,2}-TWC in the chiral carbon allotrope DZQH-C36.
AI.result: Only {1,1,2} and {1,2,3} TWC charge configurations are permitted by symmetry. The {1,1,2}-TWC is realizable in 166 spinless and 70 spinful MSGs, while the previously unreported {1,2,3}-TWC occurs in 10 MSGs for both spinless and spinful cases. The {1,2,3}-TWC is confirmed in a tight-binding model, and the first electronic realization of {1,1,2}-TWC is found in DZQH-C36 with three collinear Weyl nodes producing a characteristic S-shaped surface Fermi arc pattern.
AI.conclusion: This work establishes the complete symmetry classification of triplet Weyl complexes, revealing novel topological semimetal states with mixed chiral charges. The findings provide a concrete roadmap for discovering TWC materials and open avenues for exploring the unique physics of compensated Weyl systems with imbalanced chiral charge configurations.

title: Breakdown of Anomalous Hall Scaling in Dilute Kondo System
summary: The confluence of strong electronic correlations and Berry curvature-driven transport constitutes a largely underexplored frontier in quantum materials research, particularly in systems where electronic correlations arise from flat-band physics rather than conventional $f$-electron states. Here, we report an intrinsic Berry curvature driven anomalous Hall transport in the dilute Kondo system Ru$_2$Mn$_{0.5}$Ti$_{0.5}$Ge, a non-$f$-electron Heusler alloy hosting flat bands with van Hove singularity proximate to the Fermi level. The anomalous Hall response is strikingly non-monotonic, violating the Fermi-liquid scaling relation near the magnetic transition and is restored only at low temperature, coincident with the onset of Kondo coherence. \textit{Ab initio} calculations strongly establish that the Berry curvature originates from the Kondo hybridization induced interplay of flat bands and spin-orbit coupling mediated anticrossings at the Fermi level. Our findings demonstrate that Kondo coherence of flat bands bears a profound impact on Berry curvature associated ferroic responses, mandating a rigorous theoretical understanding of anomalous transport in the regime where reciprocal space topology and strong correlations are intrinsically intertwined.

The anomalous Hall response is non-monotonic, violating Fermi-liquid scaling near the magnetic transition but restored at low temperature with Kondo coherence onset. Ab initio calculations show Berry curvature arises from Kondo hybridization-induced interplay of flat bands and spin-orbit coupling anticrossings.
AI.motivation: To explore the largely underexplored frontier of strong electronic correlations (arising from flat-band physics, not f-electron states) coupled with Berry curvature-driven transport in quantum materials, and to understand how Kondo coherence affects anomalous transport when topology and correlations intertwine.
AI.method: Experimental measurement of anomalous Hall transport in Ru₂Mn₀.₅Ti₀.₅Ge, combined with ab initio calculations to establish the origin of Berry curvature from Kondo hybridization-induced interplay of flat bands and spin-orbit coupling-mediated anticrossings at the Fermi level.
AI.result: An intrinsic anomalous Hall response was observed that is non-monotonic and violates Fermi-liquid scaling near the magnetic transition, but is restored at low temperature coincident with Kondo coherence onset. Calculations confirm Berry curvature originates from flat-band and spin-orbit coupling anticrossings driven by Kondo hybridization.
AI.conclusion: Kondo coherence of flat bands has a profound impact on Berry curvature-associated ferroic responses, mandating rigorous theoretical understanding of anomalous transport in the regime where reciprocal space topology and strong correlations are intrinsically intertwined.

title: Universal Thermodynamic Law Governing Stochastic Pendulum Clocks
summary: Clocks' performance, especially their precision, is fundamentally limited by thermodynamic laws as they are physical devices. Yet, it is known that the established thermodynamic uncertainty relation (TUR), which imposes an upper bound on the uncertainty product of the precision of oscillations and entropy production, is violated for underdamped systems such as stochastic pendulum clocks. Here, we show that for a general class of stochastic pendulum clocks described as a weakly nonlinear oscillator the uncertainty product of the phase of a pendulum clock and entropy production takes a universal and simple form that depends solely on the degree of nonlinearity. Its validity and limitations are examined using several representative models of pendulum clocks. Our framework reveals a universal thermodynamic principle governing stochastic pendulum clocks beyond the conventional TUR and provides a foundation for designing optimal pendulum clocks that operate efficiently in stochastic environments.

AI.tldr: This paper derives a universal thermodynamic uncertainty relation for stochastic pendulum clocks, showing that the product of phase uncertainty and entropy production follows a simple form depending only on the degree of nonlinearity, going beyond the conventional TUR which fails for underdamped systems.
AI.motivation: Conventional thermodynamic uncertainty relations (TURs) impose bounds on precision versus entropy production but are violated for underdamped systems like stochastic pendulum clocks. A general thermodynamic principle governing clock precision in such systems was lacking, limiting the design of optimal clocks in stochastic environments.
AI.method: The authors analyze a general class of stochastic pendulum clocks modeled as weakly nonlinear oscillators and derive the uncertainty product of the oscillation phase and entropy production in a universal form dependent solely on the degree of nonlinearity. They validate the framework and its limitations across several representative pendulum clock models.
AI.result: The derived framework gives a universal and simple expression for the phase–entropy-production uncertainty product that depends only on the degree of nonlinearity, correctly capturing behaviors beyond the conventional TUR across multiple representative models of pendulum clocks.
AI.conclusion: The work establishes a universal thermodynamic principle governing stochastic pendulum clocks that extends beyond the conventional TUR, offering a foundation for designing optimal pendulum clocks that operate efficiently in stochastic environments.

title: Spin-Point-Group Classification of Multipoles for Nonrelativistic Collinear Magnets
summary: Multipole moments provide a unified symmetry language for describing electronic degrees of freedom and their associated physical responses. Although active multipoles have been systematically classified for crystallographic and magnetic point groups, their classification in spin point groups, which naturally describe magnetic systems in the absence of spin-orbit coupling, has remained unexplored. In this work, we present a complete classification of active orbital and spin multipoles for all 32 nonmagnetic and 122 collinear spin point groups. Treating orbital and spin degrees of freedom independently, we identify the symmetry-allowed multipoles associated with nonmagnetic and collinear magnetic orderings and clarify their hierarchy through comparisons among the corresponding spin point groups. The resulting classification provides a symmetry-based database that distinguishes structural and magnetic contributions to active multipoles and directly identifies microscopic order parameters, including those responsible for $d$-, $g$-, and $i$-wave altermagnetism. Furthermore, by classifying response tensors within the same framework, we establish a correspondence between active multipoles and symmetry-allowed physical responses. This correspondence systematically distinguishes nonrelativistic responses that survive without spin-orbit coupling from those requiring relativistic effects, providing a unified framework for understanding and predicting spin-dependent electromagnetic and transport phenomena in magnetic materials.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a complete classification of active orbital and spin multipoles for all 32 nonmagnetic and 122 collinear spin point groups, providing a symmetry-based database that distinguishes structural and magnetic contributions and links active multipoles to symmetry-allowed physical responses, including altermagnetism.
AI.motivation: While active multipoles have been systematically classified for crystallographic and magnetic point groups, their classification in spin point groups—which naturally describe magnetic systems without spin-orbit coupling—has remained unexplored, leaving a gap in the unified symmetry language for describing electronic degrees of freedom and associated physical responses.
AI.method: The authors perform a complete classification of active orbital and spin multipoles for all spin point groups (32 nonmagnetic and 122 collinear), treating orbital and spin degrees of freedom independently. They identify symmetry-allowed multipoles associated with nonmagnetic and collinear magnetic orderings, compare across spin point groups to clarify hierarchy, and classify response tensors within the same framework to establish a mapping between active multipoles and physical responses.
AI.result: The classification yields a symmetry-based database distinguishing structural and magnetic contributions to active multipoles, directly identifying microscopic order parameters including those for d-, g-, and i-wave altermagnetism. The framework also establishes a correspondence between active multipoles and symmetry-allowed physical responses, systematically separating nonrelativistic responses (surviving without spin-orbit coupling) from relativistic ones.
AI.conclusion: This unified framework provides a comprehensive tool for understanding and predicting spin-dependent electromagnetic and transport phenomena in magnetic materials, bridging spin point group symmetry and physical responses.

title: Metallic Organometallic and Semiconducting Covalent Phases of Free-Standing $γ$-Graphdiyne Molecular Wires
summary: One-dimensional carbon allotropes combining sp and sp2 hybridizations provide a versatile platform for atomically precise quantum wires with tunable electronic, vibrational, and mechanical responses. Recent on-surface synthesis has realized the $γ$-graphdiyne molecular wire on Au(100) in two interconvertible phases sharing an identical aromatic backbone but distinct linkage chemistry: an organometallic intermediate with C-Au-C bridges and a fully covalent product with diacetylenic linkages. While experimental techniques characterize the on-surface periodicity and C$\equiv$C Raman signatures, the intrinsic properties of the free-standing wires remain inaccessible. Here, we address this gap using hybrid-functional first-principles calculations. The covalent phase is a semiconductor with a direct band gap of 2.02 eV, a polyynic bond-length alternation of 0.117 Å, and a chain periodicity reproducing experiment within -0.5%. Conversely, the organometallic phase exhibits partial cumulenization and 1D metallic behavior, with spin channels crossing the Fermi level. Both isolated polymers demonstrate dynamic stability with Young's moduli of 995 nN and 861 nN, respectively, where the C-Au-C bridge acts as a soft link absorbing 9.2% of axial deformation at +6% macroscopic strain. Species-resolved vibrational analysis identifies an effective-conjugation-coordinate band at 1408 cm$^{-1}$ for the covalent phase and Au-projected modes below 400 cm$^{-1}$ for the intermediate, offering diagnostic fingerprints for phase discrimination during thermal or chemical conversion.

AI.tldr: Hybrid-functional DFT calculations reveal that the covalent γ-graphdiyne molecular wire is a direct-gap (2.02 eV) semiconductor with polyynic bond alternation, while the organometallic C-Au-C intermediate is a 1D metal with partial cumulene character; both are dynamically stable (Young's moduli 995 and 861 nN) and can be discriminated spectroscopically by characteristic vibrational signatures.
AI.motivation: On-surface synthesis produces two interconvertible phases of γ-graphdiyne molecular wires on Au(100) with distinct C-Au-C organometallic vs. diacetylenic covalent linkages, but experiments only probe on-surface periodicity and Raman C≡C signatures. The intrinsic electronic, vibrational, and mechanical properties of the free-standing wires remain inaccessible, motivating first-principles characterization.
AI.method: Hybrid-functional first-principles density functional theory calculations on isolated (free-standing) γ-graphdiyne molecular wires in both covalent and organometallic phases, including electronic band structure, bond-length analysis, dynamic stability assessment, Young's modulus determination under macroscopic strain, and species-resolved vibrational analysis.
AI.result: The covalent phase is a direct band-gap semiconductor (2.02 eV) with polyynic bond-length alternation of 0.117 Å and chain periodicity matching experiment within -0.5%. The organometallic phase shows partial cumulenization and 1D metallic behavior with spin channels crossing the Fermi level. Both polymers are dynamically stable with Young's moduli of 995 nN and 861 nN; the C-Au-C bridge absorbs 9.2% of axial deformation at +6% strain. The covalent phase exhibits an effective-conjugation-coordinate band at 1408 cm⁻¹, and the organometallic phase shows Au-projected modes below 400 cm⁻¹, providing phase-discrimination fingerprints.
AI.conclusion: The study resolves intrinsic free-standing properties inaccessible to experiment, demonstrating that these two phases of γ-graphdiyne wires span fundamentally different electronic regimes (semiconductor vs. metal) and provides vibrational fingerprints enabling phase discrimination during thermal or chemical conversion and on-surface transformation monitoring.

title: Anomalous diffusion in porous fractal media
summary: We suggest a model of a diffusive process inside a fractal sponge structure, which is a generalization of the diffusion processes on a comb and fractal mesh structure. The sponge model is considered as the direct product of Cantor sets. It is shown that the corresponding one-dimensional diffusion process is governed by a generalized Fokker-Planck equation with a power-law memory kernel and a position-dependent diffusion coefficient. That is, the fractal structure of the medium induces memory effects and heterogeneity in the transport system. The considered model may be of interest to describe anomalous heat transport in porous fractal media.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a model of diffusive processes inside a fractal sponge structure (direct product of Cantor sets), showing that the associated one-dimensional diffusion is governed by a generalized Fokker-Planck equation with a power-law memory kernel and position-dependent diffusion coefficient, indicating that fractal media induce both memory effects and heterogeneity in transport. The model is relevant for anomalous heat transport in porous fractal media.
AI.motivation: To generalize existing diffusion models on comb and fractal mesh structures to a fractal sponge structure (direct product of Cantor sets), in order to describe anomalous transport phenomena in porous fractal media.
AI.method: The sponge structure is modeled as the direct product of Cantor sets. The diffusion process on this structure is reduced/approximated to a one-dimensional diffusion governed by a generalized Fokker-Planck equation incorporating a power-law memory kernel (indicating memory/fractional effects) and a position-dependent diffusion coefficient (indicating spatial heterogeneity).
AI.result: It is demonstrated that within the fractal sponge model, the effective one-dimensional diffusion process obeys a generalized Fokker-Planck equation with a fractional/power-law memory kernel and spatially varying diffusion coefficient, thereby showing that the fractal medium geometry induces both memory effects and transport heterogeneity.
AI.conclusion: The proposed fractal sponge model provides a framework for describing anomalous diffusive/heat transport in porous fractal media, extending previous comb and fractal mesh models by coupling memory (temporal) and spatial heterogeneity effects arising from the fractal geometry.

title: Cascade spin dynamics of excitons localized in indirect-band-gap (In,Al)As/AlAs quantum dots with type-I band alignment
summary: We investigate the spin dynamics of excitons localized in type I (In,Al)As/AlAs quantum dots with an indirect in momentum space band structure. Polarized selective photoluminescence spectroscopy, i.e. fluorescence line narrowing, under magnetic fields up to 5 T applied in the Faraday geometry is employed. The experiment reveals a cascade spin evolution process of excitons in the indirect band-gap quantum dots: an initial short term spin dynamics associated with excited direct exciton states possessing a large oscillator strength is followed by electron relaxation into the X valley of the Brillouin zone and subsequent long term spin dynamics of indirect excitons. The two step mechanism manifests itself in the distinct features of the magnetic field dependences of photoluminescence: two component recovery of optical orientation, two component linear to circular polarization conversion and the presence of the linear polarization plane rotation. At the same time, suppression of the optical alignment shows one-component behavior governed by the spin dynamics of the indirect exciton states. Within the pseudospin formalism, we derive analytical expressions that quantitatively describe the observed dependences and yield estimates for the anisotropic exchange splitting: 210 μeV for direct excitons and 1.3 μeV for indirect excitons. Further analysis using the density matrix formalism agrees well with the pseudospin model calculations and shows that the finite optical orientation at zero magnetic field is due to comparable magnitudes of the anisotropic splitting of the indirect exciton states and the splitting of the X-valley electron states caused by the hyperfine interaction with nuclei.

AI.tldr: The paper investigates spin dynamics of excitons localized in type I (In,Al)As/AlAs quantum dots with indirect momentum-space band structure using polarized selective photoluminescence spectroscopy under magnetic fields up to 5 T. A cascade two-step spin evolution is revealed: fast spin dynamics of direct excitons followed by electron relaxation into the X valley and slow dynamics of indirect excitons. Analytical pseudospin and density matrix models quantitatively describe the data, yielding anisotropic exchange splittings of 210 μeV (direct) and 1.3 μeV (indirect), and showing that finite optical orientation at zero field arises from comparable hyperfine splitting of X-valley electron states.
AI.motivation: To understand the spin dynamics of excitons in indirect band-gap quantum dots where electron relaxation into the X valley and subsequent long-term spin dynamics play a crucial role, providing insight into the interplay between direct and indirect exciton states and their anisotropic exchange interactions.
AI.method: Polarized selective photoluminescence (fluorescence line narrowing) spectroscopy is applied under magnetic fields up to 5 T in Faraday geometry. Pseudospin formalism is used to derive analytical expressions quantitatively describing photoluminescence dependences, complemented by density matrix formalism calculations.
AI.result: Two-step spin evolution: fast dynamics from direct excitons followed by slow dynamics from indirect excitons. Distinct magnetic field signatures include two-component optical orientation recovery, two-component linear-to-circular polarization conversion, and linear polarization plane rotation, while optical alignment suppression shows one-component behavior. Anisotropic exchange splittings estimated as 210 μeV (direct) and 1.3 μeV (indirect). Finite optical orientation at zero field arises from comparable magnitudes of indirect exciton anisotropic splitting and X-valley electron hyperfine splitting.
AI.conclusion: The cascade spin relaxation mechanism in indirect quantum dots is quantitatively described by pseudospin and density matrix formalisms, revealing direct and indirect exciton anisotropic exchange scales and the role of hyperfine interaction in determining zero-field optical orientation.

title: Initialization-free ultralow-power programmable spin-orbit torque logic devices enabled by chirally asymmetric switching
summary: Spin logic is of great interest for the development of high-performance, non-Von Neumann artificial intelligence chips. Of particular advantage is the programmable spin-orbit torque logic that can achieve the complete set of the 16 Boolean logic operations within a single device in an initialization-free, low-power, and scalable manner, which is, however, a challenge despite remarkable efforts over more than two decades. Here, utilizing chirally asymmetric switching, we demonstrate an initialization-free, low-power, programmable spin-orbit torque logic device that is capable of the complete set of 16 Boolean logic operations within a single device with only three inputs and ultralow power of < 1 fJ/bit. We also propose the first initialization-free, all-electrical spin-based cascading computing devices, including a half adder, a three-level full adder, a two-level full adder, and a Transfer/NOT selector. These compact and scalable computing devices are enabled by the chirally asymmetric spin-orbit torque switching of a Ta/FeCoB bilayer with a significant perpendicular Dzyaloshinskii-Moriya interaction field. These results pave an intriguing way for the development of next-generation high-performance large-scale in-memory computing chips based on chirally asymmetric spin-orbit torque switching.

AI.tldr: The paper demonstrates an initialization-free, low-power programmable spin-orbit torque (SOT) logic device using chirally asymmetric switching in a Ta/FeCoB bilayer with significant perpendicular Dzyaloshinskii-Moriya interaction, capable of all 16 Boolean logic operations in a single device with only three inputs and ultralow power consumption (<1 fJ/bit). The authors also propose the first initialization-free, all-electrical spin-based cascading computing devices including half adders, multi-level full adders, and a Transfer/NOT selector, paving the way for next-generation in-memory computing chips.
AI.motivation: To develop high-performance, non-Von Neumann artificial intelligence chips, programmable spin-orbit torque logic devices capable of all 16 Boolean logic operations in a single device are needed, but achieving full logic functionality in an initialization-free, low-power, and scalable manner has remained a challenge despite over two decades of research efforts.
AI.method: The authors utilize chirally asymmetric magnetic switching enabled by the significant perpendicular Dzyaloshinskii-Moriya interaction (DMI) field in a Ta/FeCoB bilayer. This chirally asymmetric spin-orbit torque switching allows logic operations to be performed without initialization steps. The device operates with three inputs and uses compact, scalable configurations to implement all 16 Boolean logic operations. Additionally, cascading computing devices (half adder, two- and three-level full adders, Transfer/NOT selector) are designed based on this switching mechanism for all-electrical spin-based computation.
AI.result: The chirally asymmetric spin-orbit torque logic device achieves the complete set of 16 Boolean logic operations within a single device using only three inputs, with initialization-free operation and ultralow power consumption below 1 fJ/bit. The authors also successfully propose the first initialization-free, all-electrical spin-based cascading computing devices, including a half adder, a three-level full adder, a two-level full adder, and a Transfer/NOT selector.
AI.conclusion: The demonstrated chirally asymmetric spin-orbit torque switching approach enables compact, scalable, initialization-free, ultra-low-power programmable logic and cascading computing devices, providing an intriguing pathway for developing next-generation high-performance large-scale in-memory computing chips.

authors: G Subrahmanya V. R. K. Rao
title: Tensor-Network Inference in a Field-Coupled XY Model for Portfolio Allocation
summary: We apply tensor-network methods to a field-coupled XY model for long-only portfolio construction. Daily return statistics set asset-specific fields and correlation couplings. Correlation distance, four-point Gromov hyperbolicity, and Ward clustering are used to construct a sparse interaction path. A Fourier-Bessel expansion maps the continuous angular partition function to a finite-current tensor network; bottom-up and top-down contractions then give the one-site marginals and equilibrium cosine scores. A softmax map converts these scores into positive, fully invested portfolio weights. We study five equity markets over continuous ranges of inverse temperature beta and concentration gamma, and compare selected parameter pairs with long-only Markowitz frontiers and standard benchmarks. The same-sample comparisons demonstrate a tractable route from financial time series to network-adjusted allocations; predictive trading performance is outside their scope.

AI.tldr: The paper applies tensor-network methods to a field-coupled XY model for long-only portfolio construction. Return statistics define fields and correlation couplings; sparse interaction graphs are built from correlation distance, Gromov hyperbolicity, and Ward clustering. A Fourier-Bessel expansion maps the continuous partition function to a finite-current tensor network, computed via bottom-up/top-down contractions to yield one-site marginals and cosine scores, then softmax-mapped to positive fully-invested weights. Tests on five equity markets across beta/gamma ranges are compared to Markowitz frontiers and benchmarks (same-sample only).
AI.motivation: To introduce a tractable, physically-inspired (statistical-mechanical) route from financial time series to network-adjusted long-only portfolio allocations, going beyond classical Markowitz optimization while avoiding out-of-sample predictive claims.
AI.method: A field-coupled XY model built from daily return statistics; sparse interaction graphs via correlation distance, four-point Gromov hyperbolicity, and Ward clustering; Fourier-Bessel expansion mapping the continuous angular partition function to a finite-current tensor network; bottom-up and top-down contractions compute one-site marginals and equilibrium cosine scores; softmax converts scores into positive, fully-invested weights.
AI.result: Application to five equity markets across continuous ranges of inverse temperature beta and concentration gamma, with selected parameter pairs compared to long-only Markowitz frontiers and standard benchmarks. Same-sample comparisons demonstrate tractability and network-adjusted allocation quality.
AI.conclusion: Tensor-network-based XY-model inference offers a tractable alternative for constructing network-adjusted long-only portfolios; predictive trading performance is explicitly outside scope, and the approach is validated on same-sample comparisons only.

title: Nonreciprocal plasmonic response of drift-biased two-dimensional metals
summary: We develop a nonlocal electrodynamic framework for drift-biased two-dimensional electron gases (2DEGs) with Dirac (linear) and parabolic (quadratic) dispersions, deriving closed-form drift-dependent conductivity tensors from the Boltzmann transport equation. We obtain the plasmon dispersion and near-field emission of a point dipole, revealing nonreciprocal propagation in both systems. At equal drift parameter, the parabolic 2DEG exhibits stronger nonreciprocity than the Dirac system, although we find that a larger drift parameter does not by itself produce stronger nonreciprocity: the response is set by the interplay of drift and plasmon nonlocality. As such, the combination of strong nonlocality and experimentally accessible drift velocities of semiconductor 2DEGs identifies parabolic systems as a promising platform for tunable, nonreciprocal plasmonics.

AI.tldr: The paper develops a nonlocal electrodynamic framework for drift-biased 2D electron gases with Dirac and parabolic dispersions, deriving drift-dependent conductivity tensors from the Boltzmann equation. It reveals that parabolic systems exhibit stronger nonreciprocity than Dirac systems at equal drift parameters, and that nonreciprocity is governed by the interplay between drift and plasmon nonlocality rather than drift magnitude alone, identifying parabolic 2DEGs as promising platforms for tunable nonreciprocal plasmonics.
AI.motivation: To understand and optimize nonreciprocal plasmonic behavior in drift-biased two-dimensional electron gases by comparing Dirac (linear) and parabolic (quadratic) dispersion systems, and to identify which material platform offers the most promising tunability for practical nonreciprocal plasmonic applications.
AI.method: Derive closed-form drift-dependent conductivity tensors from the Boltzmann transport equation within a nonlocal electrodynamic framework for both Dirac and parabolic 2DEG dispersions; then compute plasmon dispersion and near-field emission of a point dipole to assess nonreciprocal propagation.
AI.result: Both systems exhibit nonreciprocal plasmon propagation. At equal drift parameter, the parabolic 2DEG shows stronger nonreciprocity than the Dirac system. However, larger drift parameters do not monotonically produce stronger nonreciprocity—the response depends on the interplay between drift and plasmon nonlocality.
AI.conclusion: The combination of strong nonlocality and experimentally accessible drift velocities makes parabolic semiconductor 2DEGs a promising platform for tunable, nonreciprocal plasmonics.

title: Demonstration of room-temperature, magnetic-field-free, and ultralow-power spin-orbit torque logic device based on composition-uniform van der Waals magnet Fe3GaTe2
summary: Van der Waals magnets have received blooming interest in material science and spintronics for the advantages of low magnetization, flexible stacking, strong tunability, and dangling-bond-free interfaces. However, there has been no report of room-temperature magnetic-field-free spin logic device based on a van der Waals magnet. Here, we demonstrate a room-temperature, field-free, low-power, scalable spin-orbit torque in-memory computing logic device utilizing a van der Waals magnet Fe3GaTe2 bit with strong perpendicular magnetic anisotropy and a Pt channel with strong spin Hall effect, high electrical conductivity, and electric asymmetries. Current pulse width-dependent switching measurement reveals a low intrinsic critical magnetic-field-free switching current of 1.8e7 A cm-2, a high thermal stability factor of 50, and the potential of an ultralow write power of 1.5 fJ per bit at 1 ns pulse width for a typical industrial-level device dimensions (40 times lower than the industrially optimized W/FeCoB device). These results suggest a great potential of van der Waals magnets in dense, ultralow-power, scalable in-memory computing technologies.

AI.tldr: A room-temperature, magnetic-field-free spin-orbit torque in-memory computing logic device is demonstrated using a van der Waals magnet Fe3GaTe2 with a Pt channel, achieving ultralow write power of 1.5 fJ/bit and offering a path toward dense, ultralow-power scalable in-memory computing.
AI.motivation: Although van der Waals magnets are attractive for spintronics due to low magnetization, flexible stacking, strong tunability, and dangling-bond-free interfaces, no room-temperature magnetic-field-free spin logic device based on such a magnet had been reported.
AI.method: The authors fabricated a spin-orbit torque in-memory computing logic device combining a van der Waals magnet Fe3GaTe2 bit (strong perpendicular magnetic anisotropy) with a Pt channel (strong spin Hall effect, high conductivity, and electric asymmetries), and performed current pulse width-dependent switching measurements.
AI.result: The device showed a low intrinsic critical field-free switching current of 1.8e7 A cm-2, a high thermal stability factor of 50, and an ultralow write power of 1.5 fJ per bit at 1 ns pulse width for typical industrial-level device dimensions—40 times lower than industrially optimized W/FeCoB devices.
AI.conclusion: Van der Waals magnets hold great potential for dense, ultralow-power, scalable in-memory computing technologies.

title: Measurements of Diffusion Coefficients of CO$_{2}$ in 1-Butanol with a New Laminar Jet Apparatus and PFG-NMR, Pointing to Interfacial Mass Transfer Effects
summary: A novel laminar jet apparatus (LJA) was constructed for precise gas-liquid mass transfer measurements up to 12 bar, significantly extending the technique's operating window. It was applied to carbon dioxide + 1-butanol between 283 K and 333 K. Corresponding measurements were performed using pulsed field gradient NMR spectroscopy (PFG-NMR), which does not involve interfacial mass transfer. Fick diffusion coefficients from LJA and self-diffusion coefficients from PFG-NMR were compared in the limit of infinite dilution, where both must coincide. Both methods show consistent trends, but LJA data are systematically lower. Experimental errors cannot explain the deviations. We therefore hypothesize an additional gas-liquid interfacial mass transfer resistance. PCP-SAFT combined with density gradient theory predicts high CO$_{2}$ enrichment at the interface, and the deviations correlate with this enrichment. Whether such an interfacial resistance exists and is caused by enrichment remains to be established in future studies.

AI.tldr: A novel laminar jet apparatus (LJA) was extended to operate up to 12 bar for precise gas-liquid mass transfer measurements, applied to CO2 + 1-butanol systems. Comparisons with PFG-NMR self-diffusion data at infinite dilution reveal systematic deviations not explainable by experimental error, leading the authors to hypothesize an interfacial mass transfer resistance possibly linked to predicted interfacial CO2 enrichment via PCP-SAFT/density gradient theory.
AI.motivation: To extend the operating window of laminar jet apparatus for gas-liquid mass transfer measurements to elevated pressures (up to 12 bar) and to investigate whether Fick diffusion coefficients measured via interfacial mass transfer agree with self-diffusion coefficients from PFG-NMR at infinite dilution, where theory dictates they must coincide. Discrepancies would point to undetected interfacial phenomena.
AI.method: Constructed a novel laminar jet apparatus capable of measurements up to 12 bar; measured CO2 + 1-butanol mass transfer between 283 K and 333 K. Parallel PFG-NMR measurements provided self-diffusion coefficients free of interfacial effects. Fick and self-diffusion coefficients were compared at infinite dilution. PCP-SAFT equation of state combined with density gradient theory was used to predict interfacial composition profiles and CO2 enrichment.
AI.result: Both methods show consistent trends, but LJA-derived Fick diffusion coefficients are systematically lower than PFG-NMR self-diffusion coefficients at infinite dilution. Deviations exceed experimental uncertainty. Density gradient theory predicts significant CO2 enrichment at the gas-liquid interface, and the observed deviations scale with this predicted enrichment.
AI.conclusion: The systematic discrepancy cannot be attributed to experimental error, suggesting the existence of an additional gas-liquid interfacial mass transfer resistance possibly caused by interfacial CO2 enrichment. However, whether such a resistance genuinely exists and whether enrichment is the cause requires further investigation.

title: On the growth of operator entanglement in brickwork circuits with Yang--Baxter gates
summary: We study the operator entanglement of local operators in one-dimensional brickwork circuits whose two-site gate satisfies the braid relation; throughout this work, we call such a gate a Yang--Baxter gate. We establish upper bounds for several structured, overlapping classes of Yang--Baxter gates. We show that the operator Schmidt rank remains uniformly bounded in time for all qubit Yang--Baxter gates and, in arbitrary local dimension, for permutation gates obtained from non-degenerate Yang--Baxter maps. We also show that it grows at most polynomially for involutive dual-unitary Yang--Baxter gates and for arbitrary phase dressings of permutation gates obtained from non-degenerate Yang--Baxter maps. These results imply, respectively, constant and logarithmic upper bounds on the operator entanglement. Conversely, we construct a seven-state involutive Yang--Baxter gate without dual unitarity and a one-site operator whose exact operator Schmidt rank grows exponentially, although the corresponding operator entropies remain undetermined. Entanglement growth in the general Yang--Baxter case remains open. All proofs and selected examples were constructed by ChatGPT 5.6 Sol.

AI.tldr: This paper studies operator entanglement in 1D brickwork circuits built from Yang-Baxter gates (two-site gates satisfying the braid relation). It establishes upper bounds on operator Schmidt rank for several classes of Yang-Baxter gates: qubit Yang-Baxter gates (uniformly bounded), permutation gates from non-degenerate Yang-Baxter maps (uniformly bounded), involutive dual-unitary Yang-Baxter gates (polynomial), and phase dressings of permutation gates (polynomial). These translate to constant and logarithmic operator entanglement bounds, respectively. A counterexample shows exponential operator Schmidt rank growth for a seven-state involutive Yang-Baxter gate without dual unitarity, though entanglement entropies remain open. General entanglement growth in Yang-Baxter case remains an open problem.
AI.motivation: To understand under what conditions Yang-Baxter gates—important in integrable quantum circuits—exhibit slow (sub-exponential) operator entanglement growth, which would imply efficient classical simulability and reveal structure distinguishing these circuits from generic chaotic ones.
AI.method: The paper derives analytical upper bounds on operator Schmidt rank for various structured classes of brickwork circuits with Yang-Baxter gates, using algebraic properties of the braid relation and specialized classifications (qubit case, non-degenerate Yang-Baxter maps, involutive/dual-unitary constraints, phase dressings). A constructive counterexample is also provided.
AI.result: Operator Schmidt rank is uniformly bounded in time for all qubit Yang-Baxter gates and for permutation gates from non-degenerate Yang-Baxter maps; it grows at most polynomially for involutive dual-unitary Yang-Baxter gates and phase dressings of those permutation gates. These yield constant and logarithmic operator entanglement upper bounds respectively. Conversely, a seven-state involutive Yang-Baxter gate without dual unitarity admits an exactly exponential operator Schmidt rank growth for a one-site operator, although entropies are undetermined.
AI.conclusion: Structured Yang-Baxter gate classes exhibit dramatically slow operator entanglement growth compared to generic circuits, but this is not universal across all Yang-Baxter gates. Determining entanglement growth for the general Yang-Baxter case remains open.

title: Bias-field control of the Neel skyrmion nonlinearity in a confined nanostructure
summary: We study the nonlinear dynamics of a cylindrical skyrmion-based oscillator within the framework of a generalized Thiele model. We demonstrate the influence of an bias magnetic field applied perpendicular to the plane of the nanocylinder on the oscillation frequency and on the nonlinearity coefficient. It is shown that the field tunes the response frequency, while also producing a substantial change in the nonlinear frequency shift. We find that the nonlinearity coefficient reverses its sign as the field crosses a certain critical value. The variation of the nonlinearity coefficient with the field is clearly illustrated by the observed qualitative changes in nonlinear amplitude-frequency responses. Controlling the nonlinear properties of a skyrmion oscillator by changing the bias magnetic field opens up prospects for creating tunable computational elements for neuromorphic applications.

AI.tldr: The paper studies a cylindrical skyrmion-based oscillator using a generalized Thiele model, showing that a perpendicular bias magnetic field tunes the oscillation frequency and dramatically alters the nonlinearity coefficient. The nonlinearity coefficient reverses sign at a critical field value, leading to qualitative changes in nonlinear amplitude-frequency responses, with implications for tunable neuromorphic computing elements.
AI.motivation: To understand and control the nonlinear dynamics of skyrmion-based oscillators, particularly how an external bias magnetic field can tune their oscillation frequency and nonlinear properties, which is essential for developing tunable computational elements for neuromorphic applications.
AI.method: A generalized Thiele model is employed to analyze the nonlinear dynamics of a cylindrical skyrmion oscillator. The influence of a bias magnetic field applied perpendicular to the nanocylinder plane is systematically examined with respect to oscillation frequency and the nonlinearity coefficient, including mapping of qualitative changes in nonlinear amplitude-frequency responses.
AI.result: The bias magnetic field tunes the response frequency while also causing a substantial change in the nonlinear frequency shift. The nonlinearity coefficient reverses its sign when the field crosses a critical value, and this sign reversal is clearly reflected in qualitative changes observed in the nonlinear amplitude-frequency responses.
AI.conclusion: Controlling the nonlinear properties of a skyrmion oscillator via the bias magnetic field is feasible and opens prospects for creating tunable computational elements for neuromorphic applications.

title: Light alkali metal functionalized two-dimensional C5N monolayers for enhanced hydrogen storage
summary: This work presents a density functional theory (DFT) investigation of a two-dimensional (2D) C5N monolayer functionalized with Li, Na, and K for hydrogen storage. Pristine C5N exhibits weak H2 adsorption, while alkali-metal functionalization significantly enhances its storage capability. The C5N monolayer can stably accommodate up to six metal dopants, with binding energies stronger than the corresponding cohesive energies, indicating resistance to metal aggregation. Ab initio molecular dynamics simulations further confirm the thermal stability of the functionalized systems at 300 K. Charge transfer from the metal dopants to C5N enhances polarization and strengthens H2 adsorption. Each dopant can adsorb up to eight H2 molecules, yielding a maximum of 48 H2 molecules per unit cell and gravimetric storage capacities of 9.42, 8.61, and 7.93 wt% for Li-, Na-, and K-functionalized C5N, respectively. The average H2 adsorption energies of -0.16 to -0.17 eV/H2 indicate moderate interactions suitable for reversible storage. Thermodynamic analysis further demonstrates favourable H2 adsorption/desorption under practical operating conditions, while desorption-temperature, recovery-time, and volumetric analyses support the potential reversibility and storage performance of these systems. Overall, alkali-metal-functionalized C5N emerges as a promising 2D material for efficient and reversible H2 storage.

AI.tldr: A DFT study shows that alkali-metal (Li, Na, K) functionalization of a 2D C5N monolayer significantly enhances H2 storage, achieving up to 48 H2 molecules per unit cell with gravimetric capacities of 9.42, 8.61, and 7.93 wt% for Li-, Na-, and K-doped systems respectively, with moderate adsorption energies (-0.16 to -0.17 eV/H2) suitable for reversible storage.
AI.motivation: Pristine C5N exhibits weak H2 adsorption, limiting its practical use for hydrogen storage. The work aims to enhance the storage capability of this 2D material through alkali-metal functionalization to achieve efficient and reversible H2 storage.
AI.method: Density functional theory (DFT) calculations were performed on pristine and alkali-metal (Li, Na, K) functionalized 2D C5N monolayers. Ab initio molecular dynamics (AIMD) simulations were used to assess thermal stability at 300 K. Binding energies were compared to cohesive energies to evaluate resistance to metal aggregation. Charge transfer analysis, thermodynamic analysis, desorption-temperature, recovery-time, and volumetric analyses were conducted.
AI.result: The C5N monolayer stably accommodates up to six metal dopants with binding energies stronger than cohesive energies. Each dopant adsorbs up to eight H2 molecules, yielding a maximum of 48 H2 molecules per unit cell. Gravimetric capacities are 9.42, 8.61, and 7.93 wt% for Li-, Na-, and K-functionalized C5N, respectively. Average H2 adsorption energies are -0.16 to -0.17 eV/H2. AIMD confirms thermal stability at 300 K. Thermodynamic and related analyses support favorable adsorption/desorption under practical conditions.
AI.conclusion: Charge transfer from metal dopants to C5N enhances polarization and strengthens H2 adsorption. Alkali-metal-functionalized C5N monolayers emerge as promising 2D materials for efficient and reversible H2 storage, with moderate adsorption energies and good reversibility under practical operating conditions.

title: Polarizable Embedding for Photoelectron Spectroscopy and Photoelectron Circular Dichroism in Solution: Core-Level Ionization of Aqueous Alanine
summary: We present a polarizable quantum-mechanics/molecular-mechanics formulation for the calculation of molecular photoionization observables in solution. The approach couples the static-exchange density-functional-theory treatment of bound and continuum electronic states with a fully atomistic polarizable embedding described with the fluctuating-charge force-field. The fluctuating charges are determined self-consistently with the ground-state quantum-mechanical density and are subsequently included in the static-exchange Hamiltonian to account for the outgoing electron. The numerical behavior of the coupled scheme is validated and applied to the X-ray photoelectron spectrum and photoelectron circular dichroism of zwitterionic L-alanine in aqueous solution, using an ensemble of configurations extracted from molecular dynamics. Calculated spectra reproduce experimental profiles remarkably well, demonstrating that atomistic solvent structure and environmental polarization must be treated together to reliably model photoelectron observables in aqueous solution.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a polarizable QM/MM approach for computing molecular photoionization observables in solution, coupling static-exchange DFT for bound/continuum states with a fluctuating-charge force field for atomistic solvent polarization. Validated on X-ray photoelectron spectra and photoelectron circular dichroism of L-alanine in water, it shows that both atomistic solvent structure and environmental polarization are essential for accurate modeling.
AI.motivation: Accurate modeling of photoionization observables (e.g., XPS and PECD) in solution requires capturing both the atomistic structure of the solvent and its polarization response, which are not simultaneously treated in existing approaches.
AI.method: Couples static-exchange density-functional theory (for bound and continuum electronic states) with a polarizable fluctuating-charge force field. Fluctuating charges are solved self-consistently with the ground-state QM density and included in the static-exchange Hamiltonian for the outgoing electron. Ensemble configurations from molecular dynamics are used.
AI.result: Calculated XPS and PECD spectra of zwitterionic L-alanine in aqueous solution reproduce experimental profiles remarkably well, validating that the combined treatment of atomistic solvent structure and environmental polarization is necessary and sufficient for reliable photoelectron observables.
AI.conclusion: A polarizable QM/MM framework with fluctuating charges successfully models photoelectron observables in solution, demonstrating that solvent structure and polarization must be treated jointly to reproduce experimental spectra.

title: Markov chains at the onset of non-reversibility
summary: For a one-dimensional path graph and a lifted path graph constructed from a duplication of each of its sites, we study how a reversible Markov chain can be perturbed and gradually driven into non-reversibility. The reversible Markov chain has a transition matrix that is diagonalizable and features real-valued eigenvalues and eigenvectors. The left and right eigenvectors form a biorthogonal system. We discuss in concrete examples how the transition matrix of a non-reversible Markov chain may be diagonalizable or non-diagonalizable, and it may have real eigenvalues and complex-conjugate pairs. For a number of steady states (flat, square-wave, wedge, V-shape), we compute eigenvalue spectra on both graphs and discuss the speedup that can be achieved through lifting. We develop a Green's matrix formalism, which we use to compute Kemeny times and mean first-passage times, and which provides valuable information and allows us to interpret the results for the characteristic times.

AI.tldr: The paper analyzes how reversible Markov chains on a path graph can be perturbed into non-reversible ones via site duplication (lifting). It examines diagonalizability properties, eigenvalue spectra for various steady states (flat, square-wave, wedge, V-shape), and uses a Green's matrix formalism to compute Kemeny times and mean first-passage times, quantifying speedup from lifting.
AI.motivation: To understand the transition from reversible to non-reversible Markov chain dynamics on path graphs with duplicated sites (lifting), particularly how lifting accelerates mixing and how diagonalizability/spectral properties evolve under such perturbation. The authors aim to develop interpretive tools for characteristic times like Kemeny time and mean first-passage time.
AI.method: Starting from the reversible Markov chain on a one-dimensional path graph, the authors construct a lifted path graph by duplicating each site. They study the perturbation driving the chain into non-reversibility using transition matrices that can be diagonalizable or non-diagonalizable. They compute eigenvalue spectra for various steady states (flat, square-wave, wedge, V-shape) on both original and lifted graphs, and develop a Green's matrix formalism to compute Kemeny times and mean first-passage times.
AI.result: The paper demonstrates in concrete examples that non-reversible Markov chain transition matrices may be diagonalizable or not, and may feature real eigenvalues or complex-conjugate pairs. The spectral computations across multiple steady states and the Green's matrix formalism yield Kemeny times and mean first-passage times, revealing speedup achievable through lifting on both graphs.
AI.conclusion: Lifting provides a mechanism to accelerate mixing in Markov chains on path graphs. The Green's matrix formalism offers a valuable framework for interpreting characteristic times, and the analysis of eigenvalue spectra across different steady states clarifies the influence of non-reversibility on convergence and first-passage behavior.

title: ANT:UI: An interactive 3D tool for preparing ANT.Gaussian molecular junction geometries
summary: ANT.UI is a Python graphical interface that automates the construction of molecular-junction geometries for NEGF-DFT quantum transport calculations. Through a real-time 3D viewer, users interactively position electrodes and molecules and generate complete, ready-to-run input files for Gaussian and ANT.Gaussian without manual scripting. Dedicated Pull, Grid, and Rotation assistants further automate electrode-pulling sequences, surface scans, and step-wise rotation studies, with optional geometry-optimisation chaining across each sequence. By replacing a process that previously demanded days of custom scripting with a point-and-click workflow, ANT.UI accelerates research in theoretical molecular electronics and lowers the barrier to entry for new users. The software also exports all constructed geometries in standard XYZ format, allowing direct reuse in molecular dynamics codes or third-party visualization tools without manual reformatting.

AI.tldr: ANT.UI is a Python graphical interface that automates the construction of molecular-junction geometries for NEGF-DFT quantum transport calculations, replacing days of custom scripting with a point-and-click workflow featuring a real-time 3D viewer and assistants for electrode positioning, pulling, surface scans, and rotation studies.
AI.motivation: Building molecular-junction geometries for NEGF-DFT quantum transport calculations previously required days of custom scripting, which slowed research in theoretical molecular electronics and created a high barrier to entry for new users.
AI.method: ANT.UI provides a Python-based GUI with a real-time 3D viewer enabling interactive positioning of electrodes and molecules. It includes dedicated Pull, Grid, and Rotation assistants for automating electrode-pulling sequences, surface scans, and step-wise rotation studies, with optional geometry-optimisation chaining across sequences. It generates ready-to-run input files for Gaussian and ANT.Gaussian, and exports geometries in standard XYZ format.
AI.result: The software automates the entire geometry construction process, eliminating manual scripting, and produces complete input files for quantum transport calculations. Exported XYZ geometries allow direct reuse in molecular dynamics codes or third-party visualization tools.
AI.conclusion: ANT.UI accelerates theoretical molecular electronics research by converting a previously labour-intensive, script-heavy process into an intuitive point-and-click workflow, lowering the barrier to entry and enabling broader adoption.

title: Hydrogen Storage on Transition-Metal-Decorated Nitrogen-Modified Carbon Nanoribbons
summary: Recently synthesized carbon nanoribbons (CNRs) were investigated for hydrogen (H2) storage using first-principles density functional theory calculations. Pristine CNRs exhibited weak H2 adsorption; therefore, the host structure was modified by substituting carbon atoms at the C-H edges with 12 nitrogen atoms, followed by Mn and Y doping to enhance H2 binding. A maximum of five metal atoms could be accommodated on the 12N-CNRs. Electronic structure analysis revealed strong orbital hybridization between the metal atoms and the CNRs, while binding energy calculations confirmed the structural stability of the doped systems. Bader charge analysis further quantified the charge transfer between the metal atoms and the host structure. The average H2 adsorption energies were calculated to be -0.40 eV/H2 for the Mn-doped system and -0.25 eV/H2 for the Y-doped system, which are within the desirable range for reversible hydrogen storage. The maximum theoretical gravimetric storage capacities at 0 K reached 7.48 wt% for the Mn-doped system and 6.55 wt% for the Y-doped system. Under practical conditions of 30 atm and 298.15 K, the storage capacity of the Y-doped system decreased to 6.04 wt%, whereas the Mn-doped system maintained its full capacity of 7.48 wt%. Thermodynamic analysis indicated that H2 adsorption is favored at low temperatures and high pressures, while desorption becomes feasible at elevated temperatures and lower pressures. These results demonstrate that Mn- and Y-doped CNRs satisfy key U.S. Department of Energy requirements for reversible H2 storage and show promise as potential hydrogen storage materials under near-ambient conditions.

AI.tldr: The paper investigates modified carbon nanoribbons (CNRs) for hydrogen storage using DFT calculations. By doping 12 nitrogen atoms at C-H edges and adding Mn or Y metal atoms, the authors achieve average H2 adsorption energies of -0.40 eV/H2 (Mn-doped) and -0.25 eV/H2 (Y-doped), with theoretical gravimetric capacities up to 7.48 wt% and 6.55 wt% respectively. The Mn-doped system maintains full capacity under practical conditions (30 atm, 298.15 K), and both systems meet U.S. DOE requirements for reversible hydrogen storage.
AI.motivation: To develop carbon nanoribbon-based materials for hydrogen storage that exhibit strong enough H2 binding for reversible storage, since pristine CNRs show only weak H2 adsorption and are therefore unsuitable for practical applications.
AI.method: First-principles density functional theory (DFT) calculations were used to modify CNRs by substituting 12 carbon atoms at the C-H edges with nitrogen atoms, followed by Mn and Y metal doping. Electronic structure analysis, binding energy calculations, Bader charge analysis, and thermodynamic analysis were employed to assess H2 adsorption properties and storage capacities.
AI.result: The Mn-doped system exhibited an average H2 adsorption energy of -0.40 eV/H2 and a maximum theoretical gravimetric capacity of 7.48 wt% (maintained fully at 30 atm and 298.15 K). The Y-doped system showed an adsorption energy of -0.25 eV/H2, with capacities of 6.55 wt% at 0 K and 6.04 wt% under practical conditions. Thermodynamic analysis confirmed favorable adsorption at low temperatures/high pressures and feasible desorption at elevated temperatures/lower pressures.
AI.conclusion: Both Mn- and Y-doped CNRs satisfy key U.S. Department of Energy targets for reversible hydrogen storage, and the Mn-doped system in particular shows promise as a hydrogen storage material under near-ambient conditions.
